presenter_passages.passage_exact: Morgan has a plausible Harbor proposal: add a free digital-skills session next month. The room note is current. The attendance note suggests interest. The facilitator is still available for review, not confirmed.
Next we will make the pending work visible without turning a phone notification into a second control room.

offscreen_narration.text:
A colleague suggests paying for a small printing run to test flyers. The amount sounds minor. Morgan stops at the word 'paying.' A recommendation can sit in the brief. A purchase needs a separate human decision. The same paper workflow now has two questions: should Harbor propose the session, and should anyone authorize a specific expense?

Chapter Seventeen's Spend Envelope names amount, counterparty, purpose, execution window, retry limit, trace, and approval. The workbook adds currency, requesting role, forbidden actions, and revocation. In the Harbor case, use a proposed forty-dollar print test with the course printer and a two-day window. The number is classroom arithmetic, not a quote, budget, or authorization. The envelope is incomplete until the actual approving human can see the evidence and exact terms. It cannot be stretched into a recurring charge or an 'up to' range.

Harbor's preparation role has no payment authority. It may draft a spend request; it cannot place an order, enter a card, increase a cap, or trigger paid API usage. Put a closed gate between the proposed envelope and any dollar-moving verb. If the cost, vendor, window, or evidence changes, the paper envelope goes back to Morgan. If it expires, it stays closed. A prior approval of the session idea would not approve the print order. The approval has to match the action.

Now write the decision Morgan actually owns. Chapter Eighteen uses five sections: context, options, recommendation, reversibility, and what would change our mind. Option A is to propose a session subject to facilitator confirmation. Option B is to hold the proposal and gather a fresh staffing commitment. Give B a fair case: it protects Harbor from promising a session it cannot staff. The recommendation can favor A only if the brief clearly carries that condition. Morgan can also choose hold. The agent's framing must leave room for disagreement.

Put the spend question on its own line. Even if Morgan favors a conditional session proposal, the print request remains held. The brief should name Morgan as decision owner, the course deadline, the evidence gap, and what can be reversed. A draft brief can be withdrawn. A flyer sent into the community cannot be pulled back with the same ease. That difference is why preparation and side effects have different gates. An honest decision brief makes the strongest alternative visible and tells the reviewer what evidence would overturn the recommendation.

Pause. Which sentence in the brief would stop 'available for review' from becoming 'confirmed'?

Fill a Spend Envelope, then a Decision Brief. Give the envelope an exact illustrative amount, named course counterparty, purpose, window, one-or-zero retry limit, trace, human approver, and revocation condition. Mark it unapproved. Give the brief two real options, a fair case for the rejected option, a recommendation, reversibility, evidence gap, and a hold outcome. Keep the facilitator unconfirmed. Use a fictional or approved example. Do not use private operational data, open a checkout, use a card, call a provider, or publish a session.

Save revision ten as a draft. Morgan has two distinct decisions and the evidence for both. Neither has been exercised.

gates: purpose-specific L09-L12 look and voice approval
fresh provider quote, balance and enforceable one-job and batch caps
native audio timing and sentence-level edit audit
caption, diagram alt, mobile/desktop and final MP4 review
stop_conditions: source, rights, identity, voice or packet drift
uncertain job outcome or provider error; no retry
cost cap uncertainty or unexpected debit
narration omission, repetition or altered meaning
visual clipping, label collision or unreadable captions
